topic: Pilates props: ball, ring and band

slides.headline: Ball, ring, band: what are they for?
slides.sub: The small props in Pilates each do a different job.

slides.title: The small ball: feedback and support
slides.body: A soft, half-inflated ball can sit behind your back, between your knees or under your pelvis. It gives you something to feel against, which makes it easier to notice what's moving and what's staying steady.

slides.title: The ring: a gentle squeeze target
slides.body: The Pilates ring (sometimes called a magic circle) adds light resistance when you press it between your hands or thighs. It's handy for waking up inner thighs, chest and arms without heavy load.

slides.title: The band: resistance you can adjust
slides.body: Bands let you change the challenge just by shortening your grip or swapping colours. They suit shoulders, hips and ankles, and they fit in a drawer, so your home program can travel with you.

slides.title: Props can make it easier, too
slides.body: A common myth is that props only make exercises tougher. Often they do the opposite: a ball under your head or a band assisting a roll-up can help you learn a movement well before you load it up.

slides.title: Start with one prop at home
slides.body: Pick the prop that matches your goals, learn two or three exercises with it properly, then build up. A band and a small ball cost little and cover most home routines between sessions.

slides.headline: Not sure which prop suits you?
slides.body: Our Pilates team can show you how to use each prop safely and build them into a program that suits your body. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
That little ball, the ring and the stretchy band in Pilates aren't just there for decoration.

Each prop does a different job. The small ball gives you feedback, so you can feel what's moving and what's staying steady. The ring adds light resistance for inner thighs, chest and arms. Bands let you adjust the challenge in seconds and pack easily for a home program.

And props don't only make exercises harder. Often they make a movement more accessible, so you can learn it well before adding load.

topic: Posture braces: are they worth it?

slides.headline: Thinking of buying a posture brace?
slides.sub: What they can do, what they can't, and what tends to help more.

slides.title: What a brace actually does
slides.body: Most posture braces pull your shoulders back with straps. Mainly, they act as a reminder: you feel the tug when you slump. They don't strengthen anything on their own while you wear them.

slides.title: A reminder, not a long-term plan
slides.body: Some people find a brace handy for an hour here and there while they build new habits. Wearing one all day, every day, tends to swap one fixed position for another, and stillness is often the real issue.

slides.title: Movement beats any single position
slides.body: Your spine usually feels better when it changes position often. Set a reminder to stand, reach overhead, turn your upper back side to side and walk to refill your water bottle through the day.

slides.title: Build the muscles that hold you up
slides.body: Rows, band pull-aparts and upper back extensions over a rolled towel build the strength to sit and stand comfortably for longer. Twice a week is a good starting point, with chiropractic care as one helpful tool alongside.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Upper back or neck pain with arm pain, pins and needles, weakness, unexplained weight loss, or pain that wakes you at night and keeps building is worth an assessment rather than a new gadget.

slides.headline: Want a plan instead of straps?
slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how you sit, move and work, then combine hands-on care with simple exercises you can keep up. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Thinking about buying a posture brace? Read this first.

Most braces work as a reminder. You feel the straps tug when you slump, which can be handy for short stints while you build new habits. But they don't strengthen anything while you wear them, and wearing one all day can swap one fixed position for another.

What tends to help more: changing position often, plus a couple of short upper back strength sessions each week. Rows, band pull-aparts and towel extensions are a good place to start. Chiropractic care can be one helpful tool alongside that.

Arm pain, pins and needles, weakness or pain that wakes you at night is worth getting checked. Our chiropractors are happy to help. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Boxing classes: shoulders and wrists

slides.headline: Boxing class leaving your wrists sore?
slides.sub: Simple tweaks for shoulders and wrists so you can keep punching.

slides.title: Wrap and glove up properly
slides.body: Hand wraps support the small joints of your wrist and hand. Wrap snugly, but not so tight that your fingers tingle, and pick gloves that fit well. Hitting pads bare-handed often leaves wrists sore.

slides.title: Keep a straight line on impact
slides.body: Land with your knuckles, wrist and forearm in one line. A bent wrist on contact puts heaps of load through the joint. Slow your punches down while you learn the shape, then add speed.

slides.title: Power starts at your feet
slides.body: Punches that come only from the arm load the front of the shoulder. Drive from your back foot, rotate through your hips and trunk, and let the shoulder finish the movement rather than start it.

slides.title: Build up your rounds gradually
slides.body: Back at classes after a break? Start with fewer rounds or lighter pad work for the first couple of weeks. Add rotator cuff and grip work with a band twice a week so your shoulders can handle more.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling in the wrist or hand, pain over a knuckle after a heavy hit, a shoulder that clicks painfully or feels unstable, or numbness in your fingers is worth getting assessed before your next class.

slides.headline: Keep boxing, minus the niggles
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your shoulders, wrists and technique, then build a plan to keep you training. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Pilates for a stiff upper back

slides.headline: Upper back feel like a brick wall?
slides.sub: How Pilates gets a stiff upper back moving in every direction.

slides.title: It moves in more than one direction
slides.body: Your upper back bends forward, arches back, rotates and side-bends. Desk days mostly use the first one. Pilates deliberately works through all of them, which is often why it feels so good on a stiff back.

slides.title: Start with wide rib breaths
slides.body: Your ribs attach to your upper back, so breathing can help it move. Lie on your back, hands around your lower ribs, and breathe wide into your hands for five slow breaths before you start.

slides.title: Extension: small chest lifts
slides.body: Lying face down, lift your chest a little off the mat by lengthening through the crown of your head. Small and smooth beats big and cranky. On the reformer, the swan does a similar job with support.

slides.title: Rotation: the open book
slides.body: Side-lying with knees bent, open your top arm across to the other side and follow it with your eyes. Let your ribs turn, not just your arm. Eight slow reps each side is a good starting point.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Upper back pain with chest pain or shortness of breath needs prompt medical attention. Pain after a fall, pain that wakes you at night, or tingling into the arms or legs is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Want your upper back moving again?
slides.body: Our Pilates team starts with an assessment, then builds a program on the mat and reformer that suits your back and your week. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Upper back feeling like a brick wall after a few weeks back at the desk?

Your upper back is built to bend, arch, rotate and side-bend, but desk days mostly ask for one direction. Pilates works through all of them in a controlled way, which is often why a stiff upper back enjoys it.

A simple start: five wide rib breaths lying on your back, a few small chest lifts lying face down, then eight slow open books each side. Keep it smooth, not forced.

Chest pain or breathlessness needs prompt medical care, and pain after a fall or pain that wakes you at night is worth an assessment.

topic: Vacuuming and mopping: easier on your back

slides.headline: Vacuuming leaves your back grumbling?
slides.sub: Small changes to how you clean can make chores feel easier.

slides.title: Bring the work closer to you
slides.body: Long, reaching strokes with the vacuum or mop keep your back leaning forward for ages. Shorter strokes close to your body, with your feet moving along, spread the load across your hips and legs.

slides.title: Use a lunge stance, not a lean
slides.body: Stand with one foot in front of the other and shift your weight forward and back like a fencer. Swap your front foot every room so one side isn't doing all the work.

slides.title: Adjust the handle height
slides.body: Most vacuum wands and mop handles adjust. Aim for a height where you can stand fairly tall with your elbows slightly bent. A handle that's too short pulls you into a stoop for the whole job.

slides.title: Break the job into short stints
slides.body: Do one or two rooms, then stand tall, walk around or put the kettle on. Bending your back is normal and safe; it's usually the long, unbroken stints that leave it feeling stiff.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain with leg pain, numbness or weakness, or pain that keeps building over a week or two, is worth an assessment. Any change in bladder or bowel control needs a doctor straight away.

slides.headline: Want chores to feel easier?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how your back moves and loads, then combine hands-on care with simple strength work that suits your routine. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Is vacuuming the chore your back dreads most? 🧹

It's usually not the bending itself. It's the long, reaching strokes and the unbroken stints. A few tweaks help: take shorter strokes close to your body, use a lunge stance and walk with the vacuum, raise the handle so you can stand taller, and swap your front foot between rooms.

Then break it up. One or two rooms, a quick walk or a cuppa, then keep going.

Leg pain, numbness, weakness or pain that keeps building is worth an assessment, and any change in bladder or bowel control needs a doctor straight away.

topic: Yoga with a sore back: what to know

slides.headline: Sore back: roll out the yoga mat?
slides.sub: Usually yes, with a few smart tweaks to the poses.

slides.title: Gentle movement usually helps
slides.body: For most everyday back pain, staying active tends to help more than resting. Yoga can be a good fit because you can slow it down, shrink the range and choose poses that feel OK.

slides.title: Use a simple pain rule
slides.body: Mild discomfort that settles within a day is usually fine. Sharp pain during a pose, or pain that's clearly worse the next morning, means scale back that pose next time rather than push through.

slides.title: Swap poses, don't skip class
slides.body: Deep forward folds bothering you? Try them with bent knees or hands on blocks. Big backbends too much? Try a small cobra or sphinx. Child's pose with a pillow under your chest is often comfy.

slides.title: Tell your teacher before class
slides.body: A quick word lets your instructor offer options as you go. Gentle, slow or restorative classes are often an easier starting point than hot or fast-paced flow while your back settles.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg, numbness, weakness, pain after a fall, or pain that's worsening week to week is worth an assessment. Any change in bladder or bowel control needs a doctor straight away.

slides.headline: Keep your practice going
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your back and help you adapt your yoga so you can keep moving. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Pilates cues decoded

slides.headline: What does 'zip up' actually mean?
slides.sub: Four common Pilates cues, translated into plain English.

slides.title: 'Zip up' or 'draw in'
slides.body: This means gently tightening your lower tummy, as if doing up snug jeans, at about a third of your effort. It's not about sucking in hard or holding your breath while you move.

slides.title: 'Soften your ribs'
slides.body: If your ribs flare up when your arms go overhead, this cue asks you to let them settle down towards your hips. Think of breathing out gently as your arms move, without flattening your whole back.

slides.title: 'Grow tall through your crown'
slides.body: Imagine a string lifting the top of your head, not your chin. It encourages length through your neck and spine without forcing you into a stiff, military posture you can't hold for long.

slides.title: 'Shoulders away from your ears'
slides.body: This is a light suggestion, not a hard pull down. Let your shoulder blades sit wide and relaxed on your back so your neck isn't doing the work your arms should be doing.

slides.title: Cue not clicking? Ask
slides.body: Cues are shortcuts, and not every cue suits every body. If one doesn't make sense, tell your instructor. A different image, a light touch cue or a quick demo often helps it land.

slides.headline: Want cues that make sense?
slides.body: Our Pilates team explains the why behind every exercise and tailors cues to how you move and learn. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Ever been told to 'zip up' in Pilates and quietly wondered what that actually means?

Pilates cues are shortcuts, and some make more sense than others. 'Zip up' is a gentle tummy hug, about a third of your effort, with no breath holding. 'Soften your ribs' asks them to settle as your arms go overhead. 'Grow tall' means lengthening through the top of your head, not lifting your chin. 'Shoulders away from your ears' is a light suggestion, not a hard pull down.

topic: Ankle fracture: rehab after the boot comes off

slides.headline: Boot off, ankle feeling stiff?
slides.sub: What rehab after an ankle fracture often looks like, stage by stage.

slides.title: Your doctor's plan comes first
slides.body: Every fracture and every repair is different. Your surgeon or treating doctor sets how much weight you can take and what to avoid. Good rehab works within that protocol, not around it.

slides.title: Stiffness and swelling are common
slides.body: After weeks in a boot, most ankles feel stiff, puffy and a bit unfamiliar. Elevating your leg, gentle ankle pumps and tracing the alphabet with your toes are often a good starting point, if your doctor agrees.

slides.title: Re-learning to walk evenly
slides.body: Many people limp out of habit once the boot is off. Short walks focusing on an even stride, rolling from heel to toe, can help. Using a crutch or stick for a while, if advised, is completely fine.

slides.title: Build strength and balance gradually
slides.body: Calf raises, single-leg balance and step-ups are common next stages once your doctor clears them. Progress depends on your healing and your goals, so timelines vary a lot from person to person.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Contact your doctor promptly if you notice calf pain or swelling that's getting worse, redness or heat around a wound, increasing pain, or numbness in the foot. These need medical review, not just exercise.

topic: Stiff neck after a cold draught: what's going on

slides.headline: Did the air-con really stiffen your neck?
slides.sub: What's likely going on, and how to ease it.

slides.title: The draught theory
slides.body: Lots of people blame a cold breeze or the office air-con for a stiff neck. There isn't strong evidence that cold air alone causes it, but feeling chilly can make you tense up and hold still.

slides.title: More likely: stillness and tension
slides.body: Hunched shoulders under a vent, a long day without moving, an awkward sleeping position or a stressful week often combine. The muscles guard, the neck feels locked and turning your head catches.

slides.title: Warmth and gentle movement help
slides.body: A warm shower or heat pack can ease the guarding. Then move within comfort: slow turns, looking up and down, and shoulder rolls, a few times every hour. Keeping it completely still rarely helps.

slides.title: Rethink your desk spot
slides.body: If you sit right under the air-con, a light layer over your shoulders or shifting your desk can help you relax instead of bracing. Most stiff necks settle within a few days to a week.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A stiff neck with fever, headache or feeling unwell needs a doctor the same day. Pain after a fall, arm pain, pins and needles, weakness, dizziness, or no improvement after a week is worth an assessment.

topic: Pilates for climbers

slides.headline: Strong fingers, cranky shoulders?
slides.sub: Where Pilates fits alongside the wall for boulderers and rope climbers.

slides.title: Climbing is a whole-body pull
slides.body: Most climbing training targets fingers and pulling. That leaves shoulders, trunk and hips doing heaps of work without much dedicated training. Pilates gives those areas focused, controlled time under load, away from the wall.

slides.title: Shoulders that stay steady overhead
slides.body: Long reaches and hangs ask your shoulder blades to stay controlled in awkward positions. Reformer arm work, side-lying series and slow overhead patterns build that control gradually, with springs you can adjust as you go.

slides.title: Trunk tension for steep walls
slides.body: On overhangs, keeping your feet on the wall usually comes down to trunk tension. Reformer pikes, side planks and controlled leg work train your trunk to link arms and legs instead of letting your hips sag.

slides.title: Hips that let you high-step
slides.body: High steps, drop knees and heel hooks need hip mobility you can actually use under load. Pilates works on active range, so you're strong at the end of the movement, not just flexible on the floor.

slides.title: Balance out all that pulling
slides.body: Climbers pull far more than they push. Adding pressing, rotation and upper back work through Pilates can help balance things out. Most people start with one or two sessions a week around climbing days.

topic: Wrist fracture: rehab after the cast comes off

slides.headline: Cast off, wrist still stiff?
slides.sub: What usually happens next, and how rehab fits around your doctor's plan.

slides.title: Stiff and weak is expected
slides.body: After weeks in a cast, most wrists feel stiff, a bit swollen and weaker than you'd like. That's normal. The joint and muscles have simply been still for a while and need gradual loading again.

slides.title: Your doctor's protocol comes first
slides.body: Every fracture is different. Your surgeon or treating doctor sets what you can do and when, especially after surgery or plates. Rehab follows their plan, and we check in with them if anything is unclear.

slides.title: Start with easy daily movement
slides.body: Once cleared, gentle wrist bends, forearm turns and finger movements through the day are usually a good starting point. Warm water can make it feel easier. Little and often tends to beat one big session.

slides.title: Build grip and load gradually
slides.body: Rehab then usually progresses to squeezing, light weights and eventually pushing through the hand. Everyone moves at a different pace, so progress is guided by your doctor's advice and how the wrist responds, not a calendar.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Contact your doctor or fracture clinic if you notice increasing pain or swelling, numbness or pins and needles, colour or temperature changes in the hand, or pain that seems out of proportion.

topic: What we mean by 'load'

slides.headline: 'Load': the word we keep saying
slides.sub: What it actually means, and why it matters for almost every niggle.

slides.title: Load is what you ask of tissue
slides.body: Load is simply the demand you place on your body: steps, kilos, kilometres, hours at a desk, even stairs. Muscles, tendons and bones all respond to it. It isn't good or bad on its own.

slides.title: Capacity is what you can handle
slides.body: Capacity is how much load your body copes with right now. Niggles often show up when load jumps faster than capacity can keep up, like a sudden return to running after weeks off.

slides.title: Too little is a problem too
slides.body: Resting completely can lower capacity, so the next return feels harder. That's why most rehab keeps you doing something, just at an amount your body can handle while it settles and adapts.

slides.title: Four dials you can turn
slides.body: You can adjust how much (volume), how hard (intensity), how often (frequency) and how long between sessions (recovery). Changing one dial at a time makes it easier to see what your body tolerates.

slides.title: A simple pain guide
slides.body: Mild discomfort during exercise that settles by the next morning is usually acceptable. Pain that builds, lingers past 24 hours or changes how you move suggests easing back a notch.

topic: Does stretching prevent injury?

slides.headline: Will stretching stop you getting injured?
slides.sub: The research is more mixed than most people expect.

slides.title: The short answer: not on its own
slides.body: Research suggests static stretching by itself doesn't reliably reduce injury risk for most sports. It isn't harmful, and it can help you feel looser. It's just not the protective shield many of us were taught.

slides.title: What has stronger support
slides.body: Current evidence leans towards strength training and structured warm-ups. Strengthening muscles and tendons helps them tolerate the forces of sport, which is where many common injuries come from.

slides.title: Swap long holds for movement
slides.body: Before training, try five to ten minutes of leg swings, lunges, skips and gradually faster efforts. It raises muscle temperature and rehearses the movements you're about to do.

slides.title: When stretching does make sense
slides.body: If your sport needs big range, like dance, gymnastics or martial arts, flexibility work matters. Stretching also suits anyone who simply enjoys it. Keep it if you like it, just pair it with strength.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden pain mid-session, a pop, swelling or bruising, or tightness that keeps returning in the same spot is worth an assessment rather than more stretching.

topic: Rest days: why recovery matters

slides.headline: No rest days since New Year?
slides.sub: Recovery is where your body actually adapts to all that training.

slides.title: Training is the stimulus
slides.body: A session stresses muscles, tendons and your nervous system. The adaptation, getting stronger or fitter, mostly happens afterwards while you recover. Skip recovery for long enough and progress often stalls.

slides.title: Rest doesn't mean the couch
slides.body: A rest day can be a walk, an easy swim, gentle mobility or a light Pilates class. Low-intensity movement keeps you moving without adding much to your overall training load.

slides.title: Sleep is the big one
slides.body: Most adults do well with seven to nine hours. Short sleep tends to make sessions feel harder and soreness linger. A consistent bedtime is often more useful than any recovery gadget.

slides.title: Signs you need more recovery
slides.body: Soreness that hangs around for days, heavy legs, poor sleep, irritability, dropping performance or small niggles stacking up can all suggest your recovery isn't keeping up with your training.

slides.title: Plan rest like you plan sessions
slides.body: Most people do well with one or two lighter or rest days a week, and an easier week every month or so. Put them in your calendar so they actually happen.

topic: Muscle cramps during exercise

slides.headline: Calf cramp mid-run again?
slides.sub: Why cramps happen and what tends to help, on the spot and long term.

slides.title: It's not always about salt
slides.body: Dehydration and electrolytes often get the blame, but research suggests muscle fatigue plays a big role. Cramps tend to hit late in a session, or when you push harder or longer than usual.

slides.title: On the spot: a gentle stretch
slides.body: Stop, then gently lengthen the cramping muscle and hold. For a calf, pull your toes towards you or lean into a wall. Most cramps ease within a minute or two.

slides.title: Build the muscle's endurance
slides.body: If cramps keep showing up in the same muscle, strengthening it can help it cope with fatigue. Calf raises, squats or hamstring work two or three times a week is a good starting point.

slides.title: Pace and fuel the session
slides.body: Increase distance or intensity gradually, start long efforts conservatively, and eat and drink sensibly for the conditions. Hot, humid late-summer days usually call for more fluid than you think.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP if cramps happen often at rest or overnight, or come with calf swelling, redness or warmth, weakness or numbness. A physio can help with the exercise side.

topic: Swimmer's shoulder: training load in the pool

slides.headline: Shoulder grumbling after squad sessions?
slides.sub: Often it's the training load in the pool, not just your stroke.

slides.title: Swimming is high-rep shoulder work
slides.body: A single session can mean thousands of arm strokes. Shoulders usually adapt well, but a sudden jump in distance or intensity can outpace their capacity, especially at the start of a new training block.

slides.title: Watch the sneaky load spikes
slides.body: Paddles, pull buoy sets, extra butterfly and long open water swims all add shoulder load. Introduce them gradually, and avoid stacking several increases into the same week.

slides.title: Mix up the main set
slides.body: Kick sets, drills and some backstroke can keep you fit while giving a sore shoulder a lighter week. Breathing to both sides also helps share the load between shoulders.

slides.title: Train the shoulder on land
slides.body: Rotator cuff and shoulder blade strengthening two or three times a week helps your shoulder tolerate pool volume. Bands, light dumbbells or cable work are a good starting point.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Night pain, weakness lifting the arm, clicking with pain, pins and needles down the arm, or pain after a fall are worth an assessment before you build up again.

topic: Lower back pain in cyclists

slides.headline: Lower back sore by the last climb?
slides.sub: Bike setup, ride load and strength off the bike all play a part.

slides.title: Hours bent forward add up
slides.body: Cycling keeps your back in a flexed position for a long time. Most backs handle it well, but a big jump in ride time, like long summer group rides, can outpace your capacity.

slides.title: Check your bike setup
slides.body: A saddle that's too high or low, or a reach that's too long, can make your back work harder. Small adjustments are often worth trying, ideally one change at a time.

slides.title: Build up ride time gradually
slides.body: Add time or hills a bit at a time rather than jumping from short commutes to long weekend rides. Change hand positions on the bars, and stand on climbs now and then.

slides.title: Get strong off the bike
slides.body: Hip, trunk and back strengthening twice a week, like bridges, side planks and deadlift variations, helps your back tolerate long rides. Most people notice a difference over several weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Changes to bladder or bowel control or numbness around the groin need urgent medical care. Pain spreading down the leg, leg weakness or pain that keeps worsening at night also deserves an assessment.

topic: Clicking finger (trigger finger): what helps

slides.headline: Finger catching or clicking?
slides.sub: What trigger finger is and what tends to help in the early stages.

slides.title: What's going on
slides.body: Trigger finger happens when a finger tendon doesn't glide smoothly through its tunnel at the base of the finger. It can catch, click or stick as you bend and straighten, often worse in the morning.

slides.title: Ease off the heavy gripping
slides.body: Repeated hard gripping, like tools, heavy bags or long gardening sessions, can aggravate it. Padding handles, swapping hands and breaking up tasks can give the tendon less to deal with.

slides.title: Keep it moving gently
slides.body: Gentle tendon gliding exercises, slowly moving the fingers through a few positions, can help keep things moving. Warm water in the morning often makes those first movements easier.

slides.title: Splinting can help some people
slides.body: A small splint that rests the affected finger, often worn overnight, can reduce catching for some people. A physio can advise on fit and how long to wear it each day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP or physio if a finger locks and won't straighten, or becomes hot, red and swollen, especially after a cut. These need prompt attention rather than home care.

slides.title: Why these two cop it

slides.body: Ten minutes is plenty. Easy jog, leg swings, a few skips, then build to three or four short sprints with turns. Cold hamstrings and a first-minute sprint don't mix well.

slides.title: Train the hamstring long and strong
slides.body: Hamstrings usually strain while lengthening at speed. Exercises like Nordic curls and single-leg bridges, twice a week, help them tolerate that load. Start with low numbers and build gradually.

slides.title: Give your ankles some balance work
slides.body: Stand on one leg while brushing your teeth, then try it eyes closed or on a pillow. Add small hops side to side. Simple, but it trains the reactions a court needs.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden grab at the back of the thigh, bruising, a rolled ankle you can't walk on, or one that keeps giving way are worth an assessment rather than playing on.

topic: Kettlebell swings: hinge, don't squat

slides.headline: Kettlebell swings hitting your lower back?
slides.sub: The swing is a hinge, not a squat. Here's the difference.

slides.title: Hips back, not knees forward
slides.body: In a swing, your hips push back like closing a car door with your bum. Knees bend a little, shins stay fairly upright, and your chest tips forward.

slides.title: The hips do the lifting
slides.body: Snap your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to float the bell. Your arms just guide it. If your shoulders are lifting it, the hips aren't doing their job.

slides.title: Practise the hinge first
slides.body: Stand a foot from a wall and push your hips back to touch it. Then try a kettlebell deadlift. Once that feels smooth, add the swing.

slides.title: Pick a sensible weight
slides.body: A bell you can control for ten crisp reps beats a heavy one you muscle up. Short sets with rest usually keep your form sharper than long, tired sets.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain that spreads into the leg, pins and needles, or pain that's getting worse rather than settling is worth getting assessed before you keep training.

slides.headline: Want a second set of eyes?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios can watch your swing, check how your back and hips move, and set up a plan to train with confidence. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
If kettlebell swings leave your lower back sore, check whether you're hinging or squatting.

A swing is a hip hinge. Hips go back, knees soften slightly, and the power comes from snapping the hips forward. Squatting the bell or lifting with your arms often shifts the work to places that don't enjoy it.

Practise a wall hinge and a kettlebell deadlift first, pick a weight you can control for ten clean reps, and keep sets short. Back pain spreading into the leg or pins and needles are worth an assessment.

topic: What happens at a review appointment

slides.headline: Booked a follow-up? Here's what happens
slides.sub: Review sessions build on your first visit. What to expect.

slides.title: We check in on progress
slides.body: Your practitioner will ask how things have been since last time: what's easier, what's still tricky, and how you went with the exercises. Honest answers help most.

slides.title: We re-test what matters
slides.body: The movements or tests from your first visit are usually repeated. Comparing them shows whether things are heading in the right direction and what to focus on next.

slides.title: Your plan gets adjusted
slides.body: Exercises might progress, change or be dropped. Hands-on treatment may be part of the session too, depending on your plan and what your practitioner thinks will help.

slides.title: Bring your questions
slides.body: Jot down anything you've noticed: activities that flare it up, exercises you weren't sure about, or goals like a run or event coming up. It keeps the session focused.

slides.title: How many reviews?
slides.body: It depends on you and how things are tracking. Your practitioner will talk through what makes sense for your goals and progress, and you're always welcome to ask why.

topic: Stomach sleeping and your neck

slides.headline: Sleep face down? Your neck notices
slides.sub: Why tummy sleeping can stiffen your neck, and gentle ways to adjust.

slides.title: Why it's tricky for necks
slides.body: Lying on your stomach means turning your head fully to one side to breathe. Holding that end-of-range position for hours can leave some people stiff in the morning.

slides.title: Not everyone needs to change
slides.body: Plenty of stomach sleepers wake up fine. If your neck feels good, there's no need to overhaul your sleep. This is for people waking up stiff or sore.

slides.title: Try a flatter pillow
slides.body: A thick pillow under your face adds extra twist and tilt. A thin pillow, or none, often keeps the neck in a more comfortable position for face-down sleepers.

slides.title: Ease into side sleeping
slides.body: Hug a long pillow in front of you and put one under your top knee. It gives the half-on-your-front feel many stomach sleepers like, with less neck rotation.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain with arm pain, pins and needles, headaches that keep building, or stiffness that isn't easing after a week or two is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Waking up with a twisted neck?
slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how your neck moves and use adjustments alongside exercises and sleep tweaks that suit you. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Stomach sleeper who wakes up with a stiff neck? The position might be part of the story. 😴

Sleeping face down means turning your head right to one side for hours. Some people are fine with that, while others wake up stiff and sore.

If that's you, try a much flatter pillow, or ease towards side sleeping by hugging a long pillow and putting another under your top knee. Neck pain with arm symptoms, building headaches or stiffness that doesn't ease after a week or two is worth getting assessed.

topic: Pilates for nurses and shift workers

slides.headline: Twelve-hour shifts, rotating rosters?
slides.sub: How Pilates can fit around a body that never gets a regular week.

slides.title: What shifts ask of you
slides.body: Long hours on your feet, lifting and repositioning, bending over beds and desks, then broken sleep. The body copes better when it has the strength to match.

slides.title: Build strength for the lifts
slides.body: Pilates exercises for the hips, trunk and upper back can help you feel more capable when bending, pushing and turning. Start light and build gradually.

slides.title: Work with your roster
slides.body: You don't need the same day each week. Two sessions in a seven-day stretch is a good starting point, slotted in on days off or before a later start.

slides.title: Go gentler after nights
slides.body: After a run of night shifts, a lighter session focused on mobility and breathing often suits better than a hard workout. Adjust to how you've slept.

slides.title: Five minutes on shift days
slides.body: On busy weeks, try a short routine at home: bridges, side-lying leg lifts and a few cat-cow stretches. Something small and regular keeps the habit going.

slides.headline: Want a plan around your roster?
slides.body: Our Pilates team assesses how you move and builds a program that fits around your shifts. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Nurse, paramedic or shift worker? Your body rarely gets a regular week.

topic: Squash and badminton: knees and ankles on a fast court

slides.headline: Lunging for every shot on court?
slides.sub: Squash and badminton load knees and ankles fast. Here's how to prepare.

slides.title: Lunges, lots of them
slides.body: Both sports involve deep lunges, quick stops and sharp pivots. Knees and ankles absorb that load hundreds of times a match, often in a small space.

slides.title: Strengthen the lunge itself
slides.body: Split squats, step-ups and calf raises twice a week build capacity for the positions you play in. Add a little weight once body weight feels easy.

slides.title: Calves and Achilles need love
slides.body: Push-offs and quick recoveries back to the centre lean heavily on the calves. Slow single-leg calf raises, building up gradually, are a simple way to prepare them.

slides.title: Warm up on court
slides.body: Gentle rally, then lunges in each direction, side shuffles and a few quick split steps. Start the first game at a lower pace while you get moving.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A pop or sudden pain at the back of the heel, a knee that swells or locks, or an ankle you can't put weight on are worth an assessment straight away.

slides.headline: Keen to keep playing?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios assess your lunge, landing and strength, then build a plan for match days. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Squash or badminton after work? Those deep lunges and quick pivots load your knees and ankles heaps. 🏸

Both sports pack hundreds of lunges, stops and push-offs into a short match. Calves, knees and ankles take most of it.

Split squats, step-ups and slow calf raises a couple of times a week help build capacity. A short on-court warm-up with lunges and side shuffles before the first game also helps. A sudden pop at the back of the heel, a knee that swells or locks, or an ankle you can't walk on should be checked.

topic: Massage for climbers' forearms and shoulders

slides.headline: Forearms pumped after every climb?
slides.sub: Where climbing loads you up, and how massage can fit alongside training.

slides.title: Climbing is a grip sport
slides.body: Every hold asks your forearm muscles to squeeze hard, often for long stretches. Add overhanging walls and your shoulders and upper back join in too.

slides.title: What massage can help with
slides.body: Many climbers find massage eases that tight, heavy feeling in the forearms and around the shoulder blades. It complements recovery, but doesn't replace rest days or strength work.

slides.title: Mind the timing
slides.body: Lighter work usually suits the day before a big session. Deeper forearm work often feels better on a rest day, followed by an easier climb afterwards.

slides.title: Self-care between sessions
slides.body: Gently stretch your wrist flexors and extensors, roll your forearms on a ball against a table, and do some shoulder blade exercises with a band.

slides.title: When to see a physio
slides.body: Pain at the base of a finger, a pop while crimping, or elbow pain that lingers is worth a physio assessment. Our team can refer you across.

slides.headline: Forearms need a break?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists work through your forearms, shoulders and upper back to help you recover between climbing sessions. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Climbing again this week? Your forearms and shoulders are probably feeling it. 🧗

Climbing asks for strong, sustained grip, and steeper walls load the shoulders and upper back too. Many climbers find remedial massage helps those areas feel less tight and heavy.

Massage works alongside rest days, strength training and good technique rather than replacing them. Keep deeper work for rest days, and look after your forearms between sessions with gentle stretches and a ball. Finger pain after a pop while crimping or a lingering sore elbow is worth a physio assessment.
